_comment: Curated agronomic fact base for West/Central African smallholder farming. Every training pair is composed from these facts, so nothing in the corpus is invented at generation time. Facts here are established extension-service practice, deliberately excluding anything that varies by product (agrochemical doses) or by market (prices, yields). Where a real answer must reference a dose, the template defers to the product label and the local extension officer, per SPEC.md.

cassava.planting_material: Stem cuttings 20 to 25cm long with at least 5 nodes, taken from the middle of mature stems 8 to 12 months old. Never cut from a plant showing mosaic symptoms.
cassava.spacing: 1m by 1m for sole crop, about 10,000 plants per hectare. Wider at 1m by 1.5m when intercropping with maize.
cassava.land_prep: Ridges or mounds on heavy or waterlogged soil to prevent root rot. Flat planting is acceptable on free-draining sandy loam.
cassava.planting_position: Plant at an angle or upright with two thirds of the cutting buried, buds pointing up.
cassava.critical_window: Weed control in the first 3 months determines yield more than any other single factor, because cassava canopies late and cannot compete early.
cassava.varieties: Improved varieties such as TME 419, TMS 30572 and TMS 98/0505 offer mosaic resistance and higher root yield than most local landraces.
cassava.harvest: 9 to 12 months for early varieties, up to 18 months for late. Roots left too long become woody and lose starch quality.
cassava.processing_note: Process within 48 hours of harvest. Roots deteriorate fast once lifted.
cassava.planting_time: Plant at the start of the rains, April to June in the humid forest and derived savanna. Cuttings put into dry soil dry out before they root. In the south a second window opens with the short rains in September.

maize.spacing: 75cm between rows and 25cm within rows, one plant per stand, about 53,000 plants per hectare.
maize.planting_time: Late March to April in the humid forest, late April to May in the guinea savanna, and June in the sudan zone. The derived savanna supports a second crop planted in August for an early December harvest.
maize.fertiliser: Split nitrogen: a basal compound fertiliser at planting, then top dress with urea at about 3 to 4 weeks, and again at knee height on poor soils. Place fertiliser in a band beside the plant, not broadcast, to cut losses.
maize.critical_window: Moisture stress at tasselling and silking causes the largest yield loss of any stage.
maize.seed_choice: Hybrid seed yields more but must be bought fresh each season. Open pollinated varieties can be saved for 2 to 3 seasons with careful selection, which suits farmers with tight cash.
maize.rotation: Follows a legume such as cowpea or soybean well, which reduces nitrogen cost.
maize.harvest: Leave the crop to dry down until husks are brown and a black layer has formed at the kernel tip, usually 90 to 120 days after planting depending on variety. Harvesting green to beat rain or thieves costs both yield and storability.
maize.storage: Dry shelled grain to about 13 percent moisture before storing, which is the point where a kernel shatters rather than dents under a hard bite. Grain stored damp is where aflatoxin begins.

yam.planting_material: Seed yam of about 250 to 300g, or setts produced by the minisett technique, which multiplies planting material from a single tuber.
yam.land_prep: Large mounds or ridges for drainage and tuber expansion. Compacted soil produces short, forked tubers.
yam.staking: Staking lifts the vine into the light and raises yield materially over unstaked yam.
yam.harvest: Milk harvest of the first tuber can be taken while the plant continues, or a single harvest at senescence.
yam.storage: Cure tubers in shade before storing in a ventilated barn. Damaged tubers rot and spread rot to the rest.
yam.planting_time: Set yam from November to February in the south while there is still residual soil moisture, or with the first rains in March and April further north. Early planting gives a longer growing period and bigger tubers.

rice.systems: Upland rainfed, lowland or fadama, and fully irrigated. The system dictates variety and water management, so advice that ignores it is useless.
rice.transplanting: Transplant seedlings at about 21 days. Older seedlings establish poorly and tiller less.
rice.water: In lowland systems keep a shallow standing depth during tillering, and drain before harvest to firm the field.
rice.varieties: FARO series varieties are bred and released for Nigerian conditions across these systems.
rice.planting_time: Lowland rain-fed rice is sown or transplanted from June to July as the fields take water, later into August in the north. Upland NERICA types go in with established rains in May and June.
rice.harvest: Cut when about 80 percent of the grains in the panicle have turned straw coloured and the grain is firm but not shattering, usually 30 to 40 days after flowering. Waiting for the last green grain loses more to shattering than it gains.
rice.storage: Dry paddy to about 13 to 14 percent moisture in thin layers, turning regularly. Drying too fast in strong sun cracks the grain and raises breakage at milling.

sorghum_millet.zone_fit: The dependable cereals for Sudan and Sahel savanna where maize fails in a short or erratic season.
sorghum_millet.photoperiod: Many traditional varieties flower on daylength, so planting date shifts maturity less than farmers expect. Planting very early does not bring harvest forward proportionally.
sorghum_millet.planting_time: Millet goes in first, dry sown or on the first useful rains in June, because it needs the longest run to maturity. Sorghum follows a few weeks later. Photoperiod sensitive local varieties flower on daylength, so late planting gives a shorter plant without delaying flowering.
sorghum_millet.harvest: Cut heads when the grain is hard and cannot be dented with a thumbnail. A field left standing after the neighbours have cleared theirs carries the whole area's bird pressure, which is the largest single loss in these crops.
sorghum_millet.storage: Dry heads fully before threshing, then store the grain clean and dry. Storage insects get in through broken grain, so threshing gently is part of storing well.

cowpea.rotation_value: Fixes nitrogen and leaves the soil better for a following cereal, which lowers next season's fertiliser bill.
cowpea.spray_window: Flowering and podding is when flower thrips and pod borers do the damage. Protection outside that window is largely wasted money.
cowpea.dual_purpose: Some varieties give both grain and useful fodder, which matters where livestock feed is scarce in the dry season.
cowpea.planting_time: Planted late on purpose, July into August in the sudan and sahel, so that flowering and pod fill land in the drier tail of the season. Pods that fill in heavy rain rot and sprout inside the pod.
cowpea.harvest: Pick pods as they dry rather than in one pass, because cowpea matures unevenly. Pods left standing after they dry split and shed on the ground.
cowpea.storage: Cowpea weevil is the main storage loss and the infestation starts in the field, not in the store. Airtight storage in triple bagging or a sealed drum kills the weevil by starving it of oxygen, with no chemical at all.

groundnut.calcium: Needs calcium available in the pegging zone for pods to fill. Poor filling on light soils often traces to this.
groundnut.drying: Dry quickly and completely after lifting. Slow drying on damp ground is the main route to aflatoxin.
groundnut.planting_time: June to early July in the sudan and guinea savanna once rains are reliable. Groundnut needs a settled finish for pod fill and drying, so late planting risks harvesting into rain.
groundnut.harvest: Lift when the inside of the shell has darkened and veined and most kernels show their variety's skin colour. Left too long the pegs weaken and pods stay behind in the soil when you pull.
groundnut.storage: Store in shell rather than shelled where you can, dry, off the floor and away from walls. Damp groundnut is the single largest aflatoxin risk in the food chain.

local_names: tatase and shombo are related pepper types
tomato.season_risk: Wet season crops suffer badly from bacterial wilt and fungal disease. Dry season production under irrigation gives better quality and price.
tomato.training: Stake and prune to keep fruit off the soil, improve airflow and cut disease.
tomato.disorders: Blossom end rot comes from irregular watering and poor calcium uptake, not from an insect, so spraying will not fix it.
tomato.planting_time: The main crop is dry season under irrigation: nursery from September to November, transplant October to December in the north, harvest into March. A rainy season crop is possible but bacterial wilt and blight pressure is far higher.
tomato.harvest: Pick at the breaker stage, when colour is just turning at the blossom end, for anything travelling to market. Fully ripe fruit does not survive a journey on a rough road.
tomato.storage: Tomato does not store. The value is in shading, ventilating and moving fruit quickly, or in drying and processing it.

plantain_banana.planting_material: Select sword suckers from healthy stools, pare the corm to remove weevil damage and nematodes before planting.
plantain_banana.management: Desucker to a manageable number of followers, and prop heavy bunches against wind.
plantain_banana.planting_time: Plant suckers at the start of the rains, March to May, so the plant establishes before the dry season. Suckers planted into the dry season need hand watering for months.
plantain_banana.harvest: Cut the bunch when the fingers have filled out and lost their sharp angles, before any finger yellows on the plant. A bunch left to ripen on the plant splits and loses value.
plantain_banana.storage: Green plantain holds one to two weeks in shade with good airflow. Once ripening starts it cannot be stopped, so match harvest to the market day.

vegetables.cash_flow: Short cycle leafy vegetables turn over in weeks, which makes them the practical way to generate cash between long season crops.
vegetables.harvest: Leafy types are cut repeatedly at intervals rather than harvested once, so soil fertility must be maintained through the cycle.
vegetables.planting_time: Leafy vegetables such as ugu, amaranth and jute mallow can be sown year round wherever water is available, which is what makes them carry cash flow between staple harvests. Dry season production needs irrigation and meets the highest prices.

soybean.inoculant: Inoculating seed with rhizobium before planting is a small cost that raises nitrogen fixation and yield, especially on land that has not grown soybean before.
soybean.spacing: Rows about 50 to 75cm apart with plants close within the row, aiming for a dense even stand that shades out weeds.
soybean.rotation_value: An excellent break crop before maize. The nitrogen it leaves behind cuts the following season's fertiliser bill.
soybean.harvest: Harvest as soon as pods are dry and rattling. Leaving it standing invites shattering, and shattered grain on the ground is lost.
soybean.planting_time: Mid June to early July in the guinea savanna. Soybean planted late flowers on a shorter plant and yields poorly, and seed quality falls when pods mature into the rains.
soybean.storage: Soybean loses germination faster than most grains. Seed being kept for planting should be stored dry and cool and used within one season.

cocoa.shade: Young cocoa needs shade to establish. Mature trees tolerate more light, but full sun without adequate nutrition shortens the life of the farm.
cocoa.pruning: Prune to keep the canopy open and remove chupons and dead wood. An open canopy dries faster and suffers less black pod.
cocoa.harvest: Harvest ripe pods regularly rather than in occasional large sweeps. Frequent harvest removes disease sources and reduces losses.
cocoa.quality: Fermentation and drying decide the price you are paid. Under-fermented or smoke-tainted beans are downgraded no matter how good the tree was.
cocoa.planting_time: Field plant seedlings at the start of the rains, April to June, under temporary shade such as plantain. Young cocoa planted into full sun rarely survives its first dry season.
cocoa.storage: Dry fermented beans to about 7 percent moisture and store off the ground in a dry ventilated store. Beans stored damp grow mould and the whole lot loses grade.

oil_palm.material: Plant tenera hybrid seedlings from a reputable source. Dura palms grown from random seed give much thicker shells and less oil.
oil_palm.spacing: About 9m triangular spacing, roughly 143 palms per hectare. Crowded palms shade each other and yield falls.
oil_palm.harvest: Harvest on ripeness judged by loose fruit on the ground, not by a fixed calendar. Underripe bunches give less oil, overripe raises free fatty acid and lowers quality.
oil_palm.planting_time: Field plant at the start of the rains, April to June, after 10 to 12 months in the nursery. Planting at the end of the rains wastes a year of growth.
oil_palm.storage: Fruit does not store. Free fatty acid begins rising the moment the bunch is cut, so process within 24 to 48 hours.

sweet_potato.planting_material: Use vine cuttings about 30cm long taken from healthy vigorous vines, planted into ridges or mounds.
sweet_potato.land_prep: Ridges or mounds give the roots room to size up and keep them out of waterlogged soil.
sweet_potato.harvest: Lift carefully. Bruised and cut roots rot quickly in storage and do not sell.
common_problems: vine cuttings taken from diseased stock
sweet_potato.planting_time: Plant vine cuttings on ridges once the rains are established, with a second crop possible in the southern short rains. Cuttings taken from the top 30cm of healthy runners root fastest.
sweet_potato.storage: Cure roots for about a week somewhere warm and humid so the harvest wounds seal, then store cool, dry and ventilated. Uncured roots rot within weeks.

pepper.nursery: Raise seedlings in a protected nursery and transplant when they are sturdy. Direct sowing gives an uneven stand.
pepper.training: Space for airflow and keep fruit off the soil to cut fungal losses.
pepper.harvest: Pick regularly once fruit colours. Leaving ripe fruit on the plant slows further setting.
pepper.planting_time: Nursery from September to November and transplant into the dry season under irrigation for the best prices, or nursery in March for a rain-fed crop. Transplant at about six weeks, when seedlings have four to six true leaves.
pepper.storage: Fresh pepper keeps only days. Drying is the practical store, and peppers dried on a raised rack with airflow under them keep colour, and price, far better than peppers dried on bare ground.

onion.curing: Cure bulbs properly after lifting, with the necks dried down, before storing. Uncured onions rot in store and that loss is entirely avoidable.
onion.storage: Store in ventilated conditions in a single layer where possible. Heaped damp onions heat up and spoil.
common_problems: heavy storage losses from poor curing
onion.planting_time: Nursery from September to October and transplant in November and December in the Sokoto, Kano and Kebbi dry season systems, harvesting from March. Onion planted into the rains bulbs poorly and rots in store.
onion.harvest: Lift when about half the tops have fallen over on their own and the necks have gone soft. Onions lifted while the tops are still upright do not cure and will not keep.

fall_armyworm.identify: Ragged holes and moist sawdust like frass in the whorl. Larvae have an inverted pale Y on the head and four dots in a square on the second to last segment.
fall_armyworm.scouting: Check the whorl early morning or late evening when larvae are active, on a sample of plants across the field.
fall_armyworm.window: Damage matters most in early vegetative growth. Late infestation on a tasselled crop rarely justifies treatment cost.
fall_armyworm.non_chemical: Handpicking on small plots, intercropping to break up the stand, encouraging natural enemies, and destroying crop residues after harvest.
fall_armyworm.chemical_note: If treating, use a product registered for fall armyworm on maize and follow the label rate exactly. Aim the spray into the whorl where the larvae sit.
symptom_reports: My maize has ragged holes in the young leaves and something like wet sawdust down in the centre of the plant.
The young maize is being chewed and there is damp gritty dirt sitting in the funnel of the leaves.

cassava_mosaic.identify: Yellow and green mottling, distorted and reduced leaves, stunted plants.
cassava_mosaic.spread: Carried by whitefly and, most importantly, by planting infected stem cuttings.
cassava_mosaic.control: The main control is clean planting material and resistant varieties. Rogue out badly affected plants. There is no spray that cures an infected plant.
cassava_mosaic.misconception: Farmers often spray insecticide expecting a cure. It does not reverse infection.
symptom_reports: My cassava leaves are yellow and green mottled and twisted, and the plants are small.
The cassava is stunted and the leaves are crinkled with pale and dark green patches.

striga.identify: Small purple or pink flowered weed emerging near cereal stems, with the crop stunted and yellowed out of proportion to the visible weed.
striga.cause_signal: A striga problem is a soil fertility problem. It thrives where nitrogen and organic matter are depleted.
striga.control: Rotation with legumes, restoring soil fertility and organic matter, hand pulling before the weed flowers and seeds, and resistant varieties where available.
striga.seed_bank: Each plant sheds very many long lived seeds, so a single season of letting it flower undoes years of work.
symptom_reports: There is a small purple flowered weed growing near my maize stems and the maize is yellow and stunted.
My sorghum is badly stunted and there are little pink flowering weeds coming up between the plants.

tuta_absoluta.identify: Irregular blotch shaped mines inside the leaf, and boreholes in fruit.
tuta_absoluta.control: Exclusion netting over nurseries, pheromone traps for monitoring and mass trapping, removal and destruction of affected material, and rotation away from tomato and related crops.
symptom_reports: My tomato leaves have winding pale patches inside them and there are small holes in the fruit.
Something is tunnelling inside my tomato leaves and boring into the fruit.

bacterial_wilt.crop: tomato, pepper, and other solanaceous crops
bacterial_wilt.identify: Sudden wilting while leaves stay green. Cut a stem and suspend it in clear water: a milky ooze streaming out confirms it.
bacterial_wilt.control: No chemical cure. Rotate away from solanaceous crops for several seasons, improve drainage, and remove affected plants with the surrounding soil.
symptom_reports: My tomato plants wilted suddenly but the leaves are still green.
A few pepper plants collapsed overnight and they had not dried out or gone yellow first.

newcastle_disease.identify: Sudden high mortality across the flock, twisted necks and nervous signs, greenish droppings, sharp drop in laying.
newcastle_disease.control: Vaccination on schedule is the control. There is no treatment once the flock breaks. Local backyard flocks benefit most, since they are usually unvaccinated.
newcastle_disease.biosecurity: Isolate new or returning birds before mixing, restrict visitor access, and never bring birds back from market into the flock unquarantined.
symptom_reports: My chickens are dying suddenly, several have twisted necks, and the droppings are greenish.
I lost many birds in two days and the survivors are twisting their heads and laying has stopped.

coccidiosis.identify: Blood in droppings, huddling, ruffled feathers, poor growth.
coccidiosis.driver: Wet caked litter is the driver. Fixing litter and ventilation prevents recurrence better than repeated medication.
symptom_reports: My broilers have blood in their droppings and are huddling together.
The chicks are hunched with ruffled feathers and I am seeing blood when they pass droppings.

ppr.identify: Fever, discharge from eyes and nose, mouth sores, diarrhoea, high mortality in young stock.
ppr.control: Vaccination. Isolate newly bought animals before introducing them to the flock.
symptom_reports: My goats have fever, runny nose and mouth sores and several are sick.
Several sheep have watery eyes, sores in the mouth and diarrhoea, and two young ones have died.

storage_pests.identify: Boreholes in grain, dust beneath the bag, live insects when the surface is disturbed.
storage_pests.control: Dry thoroughly to safe moisture before storage, then use hermetic bags such as PICS that suffocate insects without chemicals. Sealing discipline is what makes hermetic bags work.
symptom_reports: There are small holes in my stored maize grain and fine dust under the bags.
When I move my stored grain I see insects on the surface and powder underneath.

maize_streak.identify: Fine broken pale streaks running parallel along the leaf, plants stunted when infected young.
maize_streak.spread: Carried by leafhoppers, often from nearby grasses and volunteer maize.
maize_streak.control: Tolerant varieties and avoiding very late or staggered planting near infected stands. There is no cure for an infected plant.
symptom_reports: My maize leaves have fine pale broken streaks running along the leaf and the plants are stunted.
There are thin light lines running the length of the maize leaves and those plants stayed small.

stem_borers.identify: Deadheart in young plants, small holes in stems with frass, and tunnels when a stem is split open.
stem_borers.control: Destroy or plough in crop residues after harvest to break the carryover, since larvae overwinter in stalks. Early uniform planting across a community reduces pressure for everyone.
symptom_reports: My maize stems have small holes with dry powder at the opening and the central shoot has died.
The middle shoot of my young maize is dead and dry, and I can see holes in the stem.

black_sigatoka.identify: Dark streaks that widen into blotches with pale centres, starting on older leaves and moving up.
black_sigatoka.control: Remove and destroy affected leaves, widen spacing for airflow, and keep the stool desuckered. Nutrition matters, since a well fed plant holds more functional leaves.
symptom_reports: My plantain leaves have dark streaks that spread into blotches with pale middles, starting on the old leaves.
The lower banana leaves are dying back with dark patches and it is moving up the plant.

cocoa_black_pod.identify: Dark brown to black spreading lesions on pods, often starting at the tip or stalk end, in wet weather.
cocoa_black_pod.control: Harvest frequently, remove and bury or destroy infected pods, prune for an open canopy and improve drainage. Sanitation does most of the work.
symptom_reports: My cocoa pods have dark brown patches spreading across them and it has been raining a lot.
Black spreading rot is taking my cocoa pods, starting at the ends.

groundnut_rosette.identify: Stunted bushy plants with small distorted yellowed leaves, often in patches within the field.
groundnut_rosette.spread: Carried by aphids, worst in late planted and sparse stands.
groundnut_rosette.control: Plant early and at a dense even spacing so the canopy closes quickly, and use resistant varieties where available.
symptom_reports: My groundnut plants are stunted and bushy with small twisted yellow leaves, in patches across the field.
Parts of my groundnut field are short and bunched up with pale distorted leaves.

quelea_and_birds.identify: Grain stripped from heads at the milk and dough stage, flocks lifting from the field when disturbed.
quelea_and_birds.control: Scaring must be sustained through the vulnerable window from grain fill to harvest. Community wide timing works far better than one farmer acting alone, because birds simply move next door.
symptom_reports: Birds are stripping the grain from my sorghum heads and lift off in flocks when I walk in.
My millet heads are being emptied while the grain is still soft.

cassava_brown_streak.identify: Yellow blotching along the leaf veins that makes a feathery pattern against the green, brown dead streaks on the green part of the stem, and hard dry brown rot in the tuber flesh. The root damage is the part that matters and it is often the only sign, so a field can look healthy and still be badly affected.
cassava_brown_streak.scouting: Cut two or three roots open before you decide the crop is clean. Foliar signs can be absent on a plant whose roots are already corky and brown.
cassava_brown_streak.spread: A virus, spread by whitefly and by planting cuttings taken from infected plants. It is not a bacterium and it is not soilborne.
cassava_brown_streak.control: There is no cure and no spray that reverses it. Plant tolerant varieties, take cuttings only from plants you have seen produce clean roots, remove and destroy affected plants, and harvest earlier rather than leaving roots in the ground where the rot worsens.
cassava_brown_streak.misconception: It is often called a rot and treated with a fungicide or a soil drench. Neither does anything, because the damage is a virus already inside the plant.
symptom_reports: My cassava leaves have yellow patches along the veins and there are brown streaks on the stems.
The cassava looked fine but when we harvested, the roots had hard brown patches inside and were not fit to sell.

tomato_blight.crop: tomato, and potato where it is grown
tomato_blight.identify: Two different diseases are called blight. Early blight makes dark brown spots with rings inside them like a target, on the lowest and oldest leaves first, each spot often ringed with yellow. Late blight makes greasy grey green water soaked patches with no clear edge, spreads across the plant within days in cool damp weather, blackens the stems, and leaves a fine white mould on the underside of the leaf in the morning.
tomato_blight.scouting: Look at the underside of a fresh lesion early in the morning. White downy growth means late blight and the crop needs a decision that day. A dry lesion with rings and a yellow halo is early blight and moves far more slowly.
tomato_blight.spread: Both are fungal or fungus like, carried on wind and splashing rain, and both survive on crop debris and volunteer plants. Late blight runs fastest in cool wet nights with heavy dew.
tomato_blight.control: Stake and prune so air moves through the crop and leaves dry quickly, water at the base rather than over the leaves, space plants properly, remove and destroy affected leaves and fruit rather than dropping them between the rows, and rotate away from tomato and other solanaceous crops. Where a protective spray is justified, a product registered for blight on tomato is applied before the disease is widespread, at the rate on the label, and your extension officer will know what is registered and current in your area.
tomato_blight.misconception: Blight is often confused with a nutrient problem because both start with discoloured leaves. Blight makes defined lesions with edges you can trace on individual leaves, in patches that spread across the field from a starting point. A nutrient shortage colours whole leaves evenly and appears across the field at once.
symptom_reports: My tomato leaves have brown spots with rings inside them, starting from the leaves near the ground.
My tomatoes went from healthy to black stems and rotten fruit in about four days after the cold wet nights started.

pepper_anthracnose.identify: Sunken circular spots on ripening fruit that darken and enlarge, often with rings of tiny black or pink specks inside the sunken area. It attacks the fruit hardest as it colours, so the loss lands on the part you were going to sell.
pepper_anthracnose.spread: A fungus carried on seed, on crop debris and by splashing rain. Wet season crops and dense unstaked plots suffer worst.
pepper_anthracnose.control: Use clean seed from a reliable source, stake the plants so fruit is off the soil, pick and destroy affected fruit rather than leaving it in the field, harvest promptly as fruit colours, and rotate away from pepper and tomato. Where a protective spray is justified, use a product registered for anthracnose on pepper at the label rate and confirm the current recommendation with your extension officer.
pepper_anthracnose.misconception: Farmers often keep the affected fruit on the plant hoping it will still sell. It is the main source of spores for the rest of the crop.
symptom_reports: My chilli fruits have sunken dark spots that are getting bigger as they ripen.
The pepper fruits are rotting with round soft patches and there are tiny black dots inside the patches.

pepper_wilt_complex.identify: Plants wilt and die in patches, often after heavy rain or in the lowest part of the plot. Several different causes look the same from above, so the diagnosis is made below the soil line and at the stem base.
pepper_wilt_complex.scouting: Pull up a dying plant and look. A dark water soaked collar at the stem base with the root system intact points to a soilborne fungus and waterlogging. Knots and swellings on the roots point to nematodes. Sudden collapse with leaves still fully green, and a milky ooze when a cut stem is held in clear water, is bacterial wilt. Yellowing that climbs one side of the plant before it dies is usually fusarium.
pepper_wilt_complex.control: Improve drainage and plant on ridges or beds, because standing water is the common factor behind most of these. Remove affected plants with the soil around the roots, rotate away from pepper, tomato and other solanaceous crops for several seasons, and use clean nursery soil. None of these causes is cured by a spray applied to the leaves.
pepper_wilt_complex.misconception: A dying plot is often treated with whatever product is available. Wilt in pepper is usually a drainage and rotation problem, and money spent on a foliar spray is money lost.
symptom_reports: My chilli plants are dying one after another, starting from the wettest corner of the plot.
My pepper plants wilt in the afternoon and by the next week they are dead, and it is spreading.

damping_off.crop: tomato, pepper, and most nursery raised vegetables
damping_off.identify: Seedlings in the nursery collapse at the soil line with a thin dark pinched stem, or fail to emerge at all. It shows up in patches in the seedbed and spreads outward from them.
damping_off.spread: Soilborne fungi that thrive where the seedbed is too wet, sown too thickly, or made from soil that has carried the same crop before.
damping_off.control: Sow thinly, water in the morning so the surface dries by evening, raise the seedbed so it drains, and use fresh nursery soil rather than soil from a bed that has grown tomato or pepper. Remove collapsed seedlings and the soil immediately around them. Do not try to save a badly affected patch by watering it more.
damping_off.misconception: The wilting seedlings look thirsty, so the usual response is more water, which is exactly what makes it worse.
symptom_reports: My tomato seedlings in the nursery are falling over at the base and the stem there looks thin and dark.
Patches of my pepper nursery keep collapsing even though I water them every day.

rice_blast.identify: Diamond or spindle shaped spots on the leaves, grey in the middle with a brown edge. On the neck of the panicle it makes a dark shrivelled band, the panicle whitens and fills poorly, and that stage is where the yield is actually lost.
rice_blast.scouting: Check the neck of the panicle at flowering, not just the leaves. Leaf blast can be mild in a crop that then loses heavily to neck blast.
rice_blast.spread: A fungus favoured by heavy nitrogen, dense stands, long leaf wetness and cool nights with heavy dew. Upland rice suffers more than flooded lowland.
rice_blast.control: Use resistant FARO varieties suited to your system, avoid heavy nitrogen in a single dose, keep the recommended spacing so the canopy dries, and remove volunteer rice and infected stubble. Where a spray is justified it is applied around booting and confirmed with your extension officer.
rice_blast.misconception: It is often answered with more nitrogen because the crop looks poor. Extra nitrogen makes blast worse.
symptom_reports: My rice leaves have grey spots shaped like diamonds with brown edges.
The necks of my rice panicles turned dark and the grains are empty and white.

soil_water.soil_testing: Buying fertiliser without testing is the most common way smallholders waste money. You pay for nutrients the soil already has while the one nutrient actually limiting your yield stays short, so the crop does not improve and the fertiliser gets blamed. A test costs far less than a season of the wrong input. Your extension officer will know where testing is available.
soil_water.nitrogen_placement: Place fertiliser in a band beside the plant rather than broadcasting it across the field. Broadcast urea on hot dry ground loses a large share to the air before the plant ever takes it up, so you pay for nitrogen the crop never sees. Placement makes a small quantity work like a larger one, which matters most when cash is short.
soil_water.poultry_manure: Poultry manure is strong and fast acting, which cuts both ways. Fresh manure burns young plants and carries weed seed, so compost or age it before use. Applied well ahead of planting and worked in, it feeds the crop and builds organic matter at the same time, which bagged fertiliser does not do.
soil_water.acidity: Persistently poor growth despite good rainfall and fertiliser can mean the soil is too acid for the crop to use what you applied. Lime corrects it but works slowly, so it must go on well ahead of planting rather than at sowing. This is worth testing for rather than guessing, because liming soil that does not need it wastes money and can lock up other nutrients.
soil_water.erosion: On sloping land, ridge along the contour rather than up and down. Ridges running downhill become channels that concentrate water, and a channel becomes a gully within a season or two. Once a gully forms it takes far more work to repair than the ridging would have cost. Keeping the surface covered, with mulch or a cover crop, protects it from rain impact.
soil_water.rotation: Alternating legumes and cereals does two things at once: it breaks pest and disease cycles that build up under continuous cropping, and it leaves nitrogen behind for the following cereal. A cowpea or soybean crop before maize measurably reduces next season's fertiliser bill. Continuous maize on the same ground is what invites striga and stem borer to establish.
soil_water.irrigation: Dry season vegetable production under irrigation usually earns more than the same crop in the wet season, because supply is short and prices are higher, and disease pressure is lower. The constraint is water access and the labour of moving it. Shallow wells, washbores and simple furrow systems are within reach of many smallholders, and drip pays back fastest on high value crops.
soil_water.mulching: Mulch keeps soil moist between rains, holds soil temperature down and suppresses weeds, which on a vegetable plot can be worth more than an extra watering. It also protects the surface from the impact of heavy rain, which is what starts erosion. Crop residues, cut grass and leaves all work; the point is covering the ground.
soil_water.cover_crops: A cover crop over the off season protects the soil surface, adds organic matter and smothers weeds before they seed. Bare ground between seasons is a loss you do not see until yields drift down over several years. A legume cover adds nitrogen as well, which makes it close to free.
soil_water.compost: Composting turns crop residue and household waste into something that feeds the soil rather than just this season's crop. It takes weeks to mature, so start well before you need it rather than when you are about to plant. Turning the heap speeds it up and kills weed seed. Compost is the practical way to build organic matter when bagged fertiliser is out of reach.
soil_water.agroforestry: Trees kept deliberately in fields provide shade, fodder, fuel and, in the case of nitrogen fixing species, a real fertility contribution. The trade-off is competition for light and water, so choose species that come into leaf out of phase with the crop, and prune to manage the canopy. Done well the field carries both; done carelessly the trees win and the crop suffers.

postharvest.grain_moisture: Grain must be dry enough before storage, around thirteen percent moisture, or it will heat, mould and be eaten by insects whatever else you do. Grain that feels dry in the afternoon sun is often still too wet, because the surface dries faster than the inside. Bite tests and the sound of grain poured into a tin are rough guides; a moisture meter at a co-operative is better.
postharvest.drying_surface: Dry on a tarpaulin or a raised platform, never on bare ground. Ground drying puts moisture back into the crop from below, adds soil and stones that buyers reject, and exposes it to animals. A raised platform also lets air move underneath, which dries faster and more evenly.
postharvest.aflatoxin: Aflatoxin is a mould toxin, worst in groundnut and maize, produced when drying is slow or storage is damp. It is invisible at levels that still cause harm, it does not go away once formed, and it gets consignments rejected by any buyer who tests. The defences are practical: lift and dry fast, never let a drying crop get rained on, and sort out every shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy nut before storage.
postharvest.hermetic: Hermetic bags such as PICS control storage insects without chemicals, by sealing the grain so the insects inside consume the oxygen and die. They work extremely well, but only if the inner liner is sealed properly every single time it is opened. A bag left loosely closed is just an ordinary bag, and this is the step farmers skip.
postharvest.cassava_processing: Cassava roots deteriorate within about two days of lifting, so process within forty-eight hours rather than harvesting more than you can handle. Fermentation during processing into garri or fufu is also what lowers cyanogen levels, so it is a food safety step and not only a flavour one. Harvest in batches matched to your processing capacity.
postharvest.tomato_handling: Most tomato loss happens between the field and the market, not in the field. Rigid crates instead of raffia baskets sharply reduce bruising, because baskets crush the fruit at the bottom under the weight above. Harvest in the cool of the morning, keep the fruit shaded while it waits, and handle it once rather than repeatedly.
postharvest.market_timing: Everyone harvests at the same time and prices fall exactly when your crop is ready. Storing well, so quality holds, or aggregating through a co-operative so you can reach buyers who will not deal in small lots, is usually the largest single price gain available to a smallholder. Selling at the farm gate on the day of harvest is the most expensive habit in smallholder farming.
postharvest.solar_drying: A simple raised solar dryer dries faster and cleaner than open ground, and keeps rain, dust and animals off the crop. Faster drying is directly less mould and less aflatoxin risk. It can be built from local timber and clear plastic sheet, and pays for itself in one rejected consignment avoided.
postharvest.packaging: Packaging is not decoration. Grading produce into uniform sizes and packing it cleanly gets a better price for exactly the same crop, because buyers pay for predictability and reject lots they must sort themselves. It also reduces damage in transit, so more of what you grew arrives saleable.
postharvest.cooperatives: Selling as a group opens buyers who will not deal in small quantities, and spreads the cost of transport, storage and testing across members. It also gives some negotiating position, which an individual smallholder arriving alone at a market does not have. The gain is usually larger than any agronomic change available in the same season.
postharvest.record_keeping: Write down what you spent, planted, applied and sold, with dates. Without records you cannot tell which of your decisions made money and which quietly lost it, so you repeat both. A simple notebook is enough, and after two seasons it is worth more than any general advice, including this.

livestock.brooding: Brooding decides how a broiler batch turns out, and chick behaviour tells you the temperature better than a thermometer does. Huddling under the heat source means too cold; spread to the walls and panting means too hot; evenly spread and feeding means correct. Start warm in week one and step the temperature down each week as they feather. Cold chicks in the first week never fully catch up, whatever you feed them afterwards.
livestock.poultry_density: Overcrowding is the most common avoidable mistake in a small broiler house. Too many birds in the space raises litter moisture, which raises ammonia, which damages the birds' airways and opens the door to disease. Growth slows and mortality rises even when feed is good. If the litter is wet and the house smells sharp when you walk in, you are overstocked or under-ventilated.
livestock.layer_calcium: Laying birds pull calcium out of their own bones to make shells, so a layer ration must supply enough or shells go thin and break. Shell quality falling across the whole flock at once points at the ration or at flock age, not at bad luck. Older hens lay larger eggs with the same calcium spread thinner, so shells naturally weaken late in lay.
livestock.small_ruminant_housing: A raised slatted floor is the cheapest disease control you can buy for goats and sheep. It keeps them off wet bedding and their own droppings, which cuts foot rot and breaks the worm cycle, since larvae are picked up from contaminated ground. Keep the house dry and ventilated but out of driving rain and direct draught.
livestock.deworming: Worm burden rises sharply in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture, so timing matters more than which product you use. Deworming on a fixed schedule with the same product year after year breeds resistance. Ask your veterinary or extension officer what is working locally, and rotate products rather than repeating one.
livestock.catfish_density: Stocking rate and water quality are one decision, not two. Overstocking raises ammonia, stresses the fish and stunts growth no matter how well you feed. Fish gulping at the surface is a warning that the water cannot carry the load. Either exchange water more often or reduce the number of fish; feeding harder into bad water only makes it worse.
livestock.catfish_sorting: Catfish do not grow evenly, and once some are noticeably larger they eat the smaller ones. Fish disappearing from a pond is usually cannibalism rather than theft. Grade and sort by size repeatedly as they grow, not once. Matching feed size to the stage matters too, because pellets too large for the small fish mean only the big ones eat, which widens the gap that started the problem.
livestock.broiler_feeding: Feed the ration that matches the stage: starter, then grower, then finisher. Switching to a cheaper ration to save money usually costs more, because the birds take extra days to reach market weight and eat for all of them. Feed is the largest cost in broiler production, so the number that matters is not the price per bag but the feed used per kilogram of bird.
livestock.layer_lighting: Laying birds need a consistent daily light pattern, and erratic lighting disrupts laying more than most farmers expect. Never shorten day length during lay, because birds read shortening days as a signal to stop. If you supplement light, keep the same hours every day rather than switching it on when you happen to remember.
livestock.local_chicken: Backyard flocks give the best return on very small capital, because the birds scavenge much of their own feed. The catch is that unvaccinated local flocks are periodically wiped out by Newcastle disease, which erases years of slow gains in a fortnight. Keeping vaccination up, and supplementing scavenging with a little grain, turns a fragile flock into a reliable one.
livestock.cattle_dry_season: Dry season feed is the binding constraint on cattle in most of the savanna, and it is a planning problem rather than an emergency. Conserve crop residues at harvest, when they are free and abundant, instead of buying feed at the peak of scarcity. An animal that loses heavy condition in the dry season spends the following wet season regaining it rather than growing.
livestock.rabbits: Rabbits suit very small capital: they breed quickly, eat forage rather than competing with the household for grain, and need little space. The failure point is housing. Hutches must stay dry and well ventilated but out of direct sun and rain, because rabbits tolerate cold far better than heat or damp.
livestock.beekeeping: Site hives away from paths, livestock and homes, with shade and water within reach, because bees that must fly far for water work less and defend more. Harvest leaves enough honey for the colony to hold through the dearth period, and a colony stripped bare will abscond. Beekeeping fits well beside cropping, since the same bees improve pollination on nearby fields.
livestock.tilapia: Tilapia breed readily in ponds, and that is the main problem rather than a benefit: the pond fills with small fish competing for feed and none reach market size. Stocking mono-sex fingerlings, or managing recruitment with a predator species, is what keeps them growing. Feed and water exchange then determine how fast.
livestock.poultry_biosecurity: Biosecurity is what keeps a small flock alive, and it costs almost nothing. Do not bring birds back from market into the flock without keeping them separate first. Restrict who walks into the pen, since disease travels on boots and hands. Feed and water the healthy birds before you handle any sick ones, never the other way round.
livestock.poultry_water: Birds go off feed long before they go off water, so a bird that stops drinking is in trouble. Clean drinkers daily, because warm dirty water grows the organisms that cause the scours you will be treating next week. In hot weather birds need far more water than feed by weight.
livestock.newcastle_signs: Sudden high mortality across the flock, twisted necks and nervous signs, greenish droppings and a sharp drop in laying point at Newcastle disease. There is no treatment once a flock breaks; vaccination beforehand is the control. Unvaccinated backyard flocks are the ones periodically wiped out.
livestock.coccidiosis_signs: Blood in the droppings, huddling, ruffled feathers and poor growth point at coccidiosis. Wet caked litter is the driver, so fixing litter and ventilation prevents recurrence better than repeated medication does.
livestock.goat_worms: Worm burden rises in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture. Pale gums and poor condition despite adequate feed suggest a heavy burden. Rotate products rather than using the same one every time, because repeating one breeds resistance, and ask locally which still works.
livestock.cattle_down: A cow that has been down for more than a day is an emergency, not a management question. Causes range from metabolic to injury to infectious, and telling them apart needs hands on the animal. Call a veterinary officer rather than treating blind.
livestock.fish_water: In a catfish pond the water is the environment and the waste bin at once. Fish gulping at the surface, feed left uneaten, or a sudden smell mean the water cannot carry the load. Exchange water or reduce stocking; feeding harder into bad water makes it worse.
livestock.livestock_escalate: Sudden deaths across several animals, nervous signs, mouth or foot lesions, or anything spreading quickly are reasons to contact a veterinary or extension officer the same day rather than treating on your own. Some of these are notifiable, and the response is a district-level one.

zones.sahel: Very short erratic season, roughly 250 to 500mm. Millet, sorghum, cowpea. Drought escape through short duration varieties matters more than yield potential.
zones.sudan: Single season, roughly 500 to 1000mm. Sorghum, millet, cowpea, groundnut, some maize with fertiliser.
zones.guinea: Long single season, roughly 1000 to 1400mm. The maize, yam, soybean and rice belt.
zones.derived: Transition zone, in places two peaks of rain, supporting an early and a late crop.
zones.humid_forest: High rainfall with two seasons. Cassava, plantain, cocoa, oil palm, vegetables. Disease pressure is high because humidity is high.
zones.planting_rule: Plant on established rains, not on the first shower, in every zone. A false start is the most expensive common mistake.

market.harvest_glut: Everyone harvests at once and the price falls exactly when your crop is ready. Selling at the farm gate on the day of harvest is the most expensive habit in smallholder farming, because you are selling into the moment of maximum supply.
market.storage_arbitrage: If you can dry properly and store so quality holds, selling later usually earns more. The gain has to be weighed against storage losses and the cash you need now, which is why storage only pays when the drying and the bags are done properly.
market.aggregation: Selling as a group reaches buyers who will not deal in small lots, and spreads the cost of transport, storage and testing. For most smallholders this is the largest single price gain available in a season, larger than most agronomic changes.
market.grading: Grading into uniform sizes and packing cleanly earns more for the same crop, because buyers pay for predictability and discount lots they must sort themselves.
market.price_variability: Prices move week to week and differ between markets, so a number quoted from anywhere other than your own market on the day is unreliable. Traders at the market, other farmers who sold recently, and farmer associations are the practical sources.
market.contract_caution: An off-taker agreement can be worth more than a high spot price because it removes uncertainty, but read what happens if you cannot deliver the volume. Agreements that penalise shortfall are dangerous in a season with poor rains.
market.input_cost: Judge an input by the extra yield it returns, not by its price per bag. A cheap fertiliser broadcast badly can cost more per kilogram of grain than a more expensive one placed correctly.

weather.no_forecast: Live weather is not something an offline model can provide. What it can do is explain what to watch for: rains that have fallen steadily for several days and wet soil below the surface, rather than a single shower.
weather.false_start: Planting on the first shower is the most expensive common mistake. A false start kills the stand and forces a replant, paying twice for seed and labour in the same season.
weather.dry_spell: A dry spell during flowering costs more yield than the same gap at any other stage. If a dry spell is likely, choosing a shorter duration variety that escapes it matters more than chasing maximum yield potential.
weather.harmattan: The harmattan brings dry dusty air that speeds drying, which helps a harvested crop and hurts a standing one. Plan drying and storage around it and protect late vegetables from the desiccating wind.
weather.flood_risk: On low lying or fadama land, raised beds and drainage channels dug before the rains are worth more than anything done once water is standing.
weather.climate_shift: Farmers across the region report rains starting later and stopping earlier than they used to. Shorter duration varieties and staggered planting hedge against a season that does not behave like the last one.

nitrogen_deficiency.identify: An even pale green to yellow colour over the whole leaf, starting on the oldest leaves at the bottom of the plant while the new leaves at the top stay greener. The plant is short, thin stemmed and generally weak rather than spotted or lesioned.
nitrogen_deficiency.why_oldest_first: Nitrogen moves inside the plant. When there is not enough, the plant withdraws it from the old leaves to build the new ones, so the bottom of the plant goes yellow first. That bottom up pattern is the single most useful thing to look at, because most diseases do the opposite or appear at random.
nitrogen_deficiency.crop_signs: In maize the yellowing runs down the midrib of a lower leaf from the tip, making a V shape that points back at the stem. In rice the whole stand looks pale and yellow green, the plants are short, and they put out far fewer tillers than they should.
nitrogen_deficiency.confirm: Look at the pattern across the field, not just one plant. A nitrogen shortage is even, follows the leaf age gradient, and is often worse on the sandy or eroded parts of the field. A disease appears in patches that spread outward from a starting point and marks individual leaves with defined lesions.
nitrogen_deficiency.correct: Topdress with a nitrogen fertiliser and place it in a band beside the plant rather than broadcasting it, then cover it with soil or apply it just before rain so it is not lost to the air. The crop responds within one to two weeks if nitrogen was really the problem, which is also how you confirm the diagnosis. Rates depend on the crop, the soil and the product, so take the rate from your extension officer or from a soil test rather than from a general figure.
nitrogen_deficiency.misconception: Yellow leaves are treated as a disease and sprayed. No spray puts nitrogen into a plant.
symptom_reports: My maize is short and the lower leaves are yellowing from the tip down the middle of the leaf, while the top leaves are still green.
My rice is pale yellow green all over the field, the plants are short and they have hardly tillered.

nitrogen_timing.principle: Nitrogen is split across the season rather than applied all at once. It leaches with rain and escapes to the air from the surface, so a single large dose at planting is partly gone before the crop is big enough to use it, and the crop then runs short exactly when it is building yield.
nitrogen_timing.maize: Apply a smaller basal portion at or just after planting, then topdress the larger share when the crop is about knee high, roughly three to four weeks after emergence and before tasselling. A crop that goes short at tasselling does not recover.
nitrogen_timing.rice: In lowland rice, a basal portion goes in at or just before transplanting, the main topdressing goes on at active tillering when the crop is putting out shoots, and a third portion at panicle initiation. Drain or keep the water shallow when you apply, then let it back up so the fertiliser is held in the soil rather than floating off with the flow.
nitrogen_timing.vegetative_adjustment: During vegetative growth the crop is building the leaves and tillers that determine yield, so this is where a shortage costs most and where a topdressing pays best. If the lower leaves are yellowing during tillering or early vegetative growth, bring the topdressing forward rather than waiting for the calendar date.
nitrogen_timing.placement: Band it beside the plant and cover it. Broadcast urea on hot dry ground loses a large share to the air before the crop takes any up, and urea scattered on wet leaves scorches them.
nitrogen_timing.misconception: Applying everything at planting is common because it saves a trip across the field. It wastes fertiliser you have already paid for.
symptom_reports: When should I put fertiliser on my maize, and should I put it all at planting?
How do I split nitrogen on lowland rice through the season?

phosphorus_deficiency.identify: Stunted plants with an unusually dark dull green colour, and purple or reddish tints along the stems and the edges of the older leaves, most visible on young maize. The crop is late to flower and late to mature.
phosphorus_deficiency.confirm: Purpling from phosphorus is uniform across the field and worst on acid or eroded soils and in cold early plantings. Purpling on scattered individual plants is more often cold, waterlogging or root damage.
phosphorus_deficiency.correct: Phosphorus has to be in the soil where the young roots are, so it is applied at planting rather than topdressed. A topdressing of urea will not fix it, and on strongly acid soil the phosphorus already present is locked up until the acidity is addressed. Confirm with a soil test before buying, because phosphorus is expensive and the requirement varies widely.
phosphorus_deficiency.misconception: Purple maize seedlings are often treated with more urea, which is the wrong nutrient entirely.
symptom_reports: My young maize is very dark green with purple edges on the leaves and stems, and it is not growing.
My crop is stunted and flowering late, and the older leaves have a reddish purple tint.

potassium_deficiency.identify: Scorching and browning along the outer margins and tips of the older lower leaves, while the middle of the leaf stays green. Stalks are weak, the crop lodges in wind, and grain or tuber filling is poor.
potassium_deficiency.confirm: The scorch follows the leaf edge as a band. A disease lesion sits inside the leaf with a definite edge, and a nitrogen shortage yellows the whole leaf evenly rather than burning its margin.
potassium_deficiency.correct: Potassium is applied to the soil, usually at planting or as an early topdressing, and the requirement is highest for cassava, banana, plantain and other crops that move a lot of bulk. Returning crop residues and using compost puts potassium back over time. Take the rate from a soil test.
potassium_deficiency.misconception: Leaf edge scorch is often blamed on sun or on a spray burn. If it is on the oldest leaves and consistent across the field, look at potassium first.
symptom_reports: The edges of my lower maize leaves are burnt brown while the middle of the leaf is still green, and the stalks are falling over.
My cassava leaves are scorched around the rim, starting with the older ones down the stem.

deficiency_or_disease.principle: Before spending money, decide whether the crop is short of a nutrient or is infected, because the two look similar from a distance and nothing you buy works for both.
deficiency_or_disease.identify: A nutrient shortage is even and it follows the age of the leaf. Whole leaves change colour, the change is symmetrical either side of the midrib, it appears across the field at roughly the same time, and it tracks the poor and sandy patches. A disease is patchy and it spreads. It makes lesions with edges you can trace, on some leaves and not others, it starts from a focus and moves outward week by week, and it often leaves a visible sign such as mould, ooze, frass or a spore mass.
deficiency_or_disease.confirm: Two field tests settle most cases. Walk the field and ask whether the affected plants are grouped or scattered evenly. Then look at whether the oldest leaves went first, which points to a mobile nutrient such as nitrogen or potassium, or the youngest, which points to something else. If it is still unclear, take a whole affected plant with its roots, and a healthy one for comparison, to your extension officer.
deficiency_or_disease.correct: Fix the cause you actually identified. A soil test is cheap against a season of the wrong fertiliser, and a correct nutrient diagnosis usually shows a visible response within one to two weeks, which confirms it.
deficiency_or_disease.misconception: The most expensive mistake in this domain is spraying a nutrient shortage or fertilising a disease. Both leave the real problem running.
symptom_reports: My crop is yellowing and I do not know whether it needs fertiliser or whether it is a disease.
How do I tell if my plants are sick or just hungry?

leaf_colour_chart.principle: A leaf colour chart is a cheap plastic card of graded green panels used to decide when rice needs its nitrogen topdressing, instead of guessing from the calendar.
leaf_colour_chart.how: Hold the middle of the topmost fully opened leaf against the panels, in the shade with your back to the sun, on the same set of ten plants each time, and read it at the same time of day. If most readings fall below the threshold for your variety, topdress now. Read weekly through tillering.
leaf_colour_chart.why: It matches the fertiliser to what the crop is actually short of, which usually means less nitrogen bought for the same yield, and it avoids the heavy blanket dose that makes blast and lodging worse.
leaf_colour_chart.misconception: Colour is judged by eye and by memory, which drifts with the light and the time of day. The point of the card is that it is the same reference every week.
symptom_reports: How do I know when my rice actually needs a nitrogen topdressing?
Is there a way to check if my rice needs fertiliser without a soil test?

cmd_vs_cbsd.both: Both are viruses of cassava, both are carried by whitefly and by cuttings taken from infected plants, and neither can be cured by any spray. Anyone offering you a treatment for either is selling you nothing.
cmd_vs_cbsd.a_tell: Cassava mosaic shows in the leaves. The leaf is mottled yellow and green in patches, distorted and reduced in size, and the plant is stunted. The damage you can see above ground is the damage.
cmd_vs_cbsd.b_tell: Cassava brown streak shows in the root. Leaves may carry yellow blotching that follows the veins in a feathery pattern, and the green stems may carry brown dead streaks, but the plant can look almost normal while the tubers are already ruined with hard dry brown patches inside.
cmd_vs_cbsd.decider: Cut open two or three roots. Mosaic leaves you a usable root under a bad looking plant; brown streak leaves you a corky brown root under a plant that looked fine.
cmd_vs_cbsd.why_it_matters: It changes when you harvest. With brown streak the rot worsens the longer the roots stay in the ground, so harvesting earlier saves part of the crop, and cuttings must only be taken from plants whose roots you have actually cut open and seen to be clean.
cmd_vs_cbsd.control: For both: plant resistant or tolerant varieties, take planting material only from clean plants, and remove and destroy affected plants rather than leaving them as a source.

blight_vs_nitrogen.both: Both start as discoloured lower leaves on tomato, which is why they get confused, and the two need completely different responses.
blight_vs_nitrogen.a_tell: Blight makes lesions. There are defined spots with edges you can trace, dark brown with rings inside them for early blight, or greasy grey green water soaked patches with a white mould on the leaf underside for late blight. It marks some leaves and not others, and it spreads outward from a starting point in the field week by week.
blight_vs_nitrogen.b_tell: A nitrogen shortage makes colour. The whole leaf pales evenly, symmetrically either side of the midrib, with no spots and no lesion edge. It begins on the oldest leaves at the bottom because the plant is moving its nitrogen up to the new growth, and it appears across the whole field at about the same time rather than spreading from a focus.
blight_vs_nitrogen.decider: Look for an edge. If you can trace the outline of a spot, it is blight. If the leaf is simply a paler version of a healthy leaf, it is nutrition. Then walk the field: grouped and spreading means disease, even and everywhere means hunger.
blight_vs_nitrogen.why_it_matters: Fertiliser does nothing to blight, and no spray puts nitrogen into a plant. Getting this wrong costs a season and the price of the wrong input.
blight_vs_nitrogen.control: For blight: stake and prune for airflow, water at the base not over the leaves, remove and destroy affected material, rotate away from solanaceous crops. For nitrogen: topdress and band the fertiliser beside the plant, and expect a visible response within one to two weeks, which also confirms the diagnosis.

early_vs_late_blight.both: Both are called blight on tomato and both make brown leaf damage, but one is a slow problem and the other can take the crop in under a week.
early_vs_late_blight.a_tell: Early blight makes dry dark spots with concentric rings inside them, like a target, usually ringed by a yellow halo, and it starts on the oldest leaves nearest the soil. It moves slowly up the plant.
early_vs_late_blight.b_tell: Late blight makes greasy grey green water soaked patches with no clear boundary, blackens the stems, and leaves a fine white downy mould on the underside of a fresh lesion in the early morning. It runs through a crop in cool damp weather within days.
early_vs_late_blight.decider: Turn a fresh lesion over first thing in the morning. White downy growth on the underside means late blight and the decision cannot wait. Rings, dryness and a yellow halo mean early blight.
early_vs_late_blight.why_it_matters: Late blight needs an immediate decision about the whole crop. Early blight is managed with sanitation and airflow over the season.
early_vs_late_blight.control: Both are reduced by staking, spacing, watering at the base, and destroying affected material rather than dropping it between the rows.

armyworm_vs_stemborer.both: Both attack maize, both leave frass, and both are commonly reported as holes in the plant, so the frass is the thing to read rather than the holes.
armyworm_vs_stemborer.a_tell: Fall armyworm feeds in the whorl, the funnel at the centre of the plant. It leaves ragged holes across the young leaves, wet sawdust like frass sitting in the whorl, and you can usually find the caterpillar itself down inside the funnel.
armyworm_vs_stemborer.b_tell: Stem borer feeds inside the stem. It leaves small round holes in the stem with dry powdery frass at the opening, and the central shoot dies while the outer leaves stay alive, which is called deadheart. Split a stem lengthwise and you find the tunnel.
armyworm_vs_stemborer.decider: Wet frass in the funnel with shredded leaves is armyworm. Dry powder at a hole in the stem with a dead central shoot is stem borer. If you are unsure, split a stem: a tunnel settles it.
armyworm_vs_stemborer.why_it_matters: Armyworm can be handpicked from the whorl on a small plot and is worth acting on early in vegetative growth. Stem borer is largely a residue and timing problem, managed between seasons rather than during them.
armyworm_vs_stemborer.control: For armyworm: scout the whorls, handpick on small plots, encourage natural enemies, and treat late infestation on a tasselled crop as rarely worth the cost. For stem borer: destroy or plough in residues after harvest to break the carryover, and plant early and uniformly across the community.

bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.both: Both kill tomato and pepper by wilting, both live in the soil, and neither is cured by anything sprayed on the leaves.
bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.a_tell: Bacterial wilt collapses the plant suddenly while the leaves are still fully green. Cut the stem near the base and hang it in a glass of clear water: a milky white thread streaming down from the cut confirms it.
bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.b_tell: Fusarium is slower and one sided. Yellowing climbs the plant, often on one side or one branch first, the lower leaves go before the upper, and a stem split lengthwise shows a brown stain in the tissue rather than an ooze.
bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.decider: The glass of water. A milky ooze means bacterial wilt. No ooze, plus a brown streak inside a split stem and a slower one sided decline, means fusarium.
bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.why_it_matters: Both need rotation and drainage rather than a purchase, but bacterial wilt spreads fast in wet soil and through tools, so affected plants and the soil around them come out immediately.
bacterialwilt_vs_fusarium.control: For both: rotate away from solanaceous crops for several seasons, improve drainage, use clean nursery soil, and remove affected plants with the surrounding soil. Wash tools and hands between plants.

nitrogen_vs_potassium.both: Both show on the oldest lower leaves first, because both nutrients move inside the plant and get withdrawn to the new growth, so leaf age does not separate them. The pattern on the leaf does.
nitrogen_vs_potassium.a_tell: Nitrogen pales the whole leaf evenly, a uniform light green to yellow from midrib to margin, and the plant is thin and short.
nitrogen_vs_potassium.b_tell: Potassium burns the rim. The outer margins and the tip go brown and scorched in a band while the middle of the leaf stays green, and the stalks are weak enough to lodge in wind.
nitrogen_vs_potassium.decider: Look at the middle of the leaf. Still green with a burnt edge is potassium. Pale all the way across is nitrogen.
nitrogen_vs_potassium.why_it_matters: They are different fertilisers at different prices, and urea does nothing for a potassium shortage.
nitrogen_vs_potassium.control: Confirm with a soil test before buying either. Nitrogen is topdressed and banded beside the plant; potassium goes into the soil and is partly restored over time by returning crop residues and using compost.

striga_vs_nitrogen.both: Both leave a stunted yellow crop on tired land, and striga is worst exactly where fertility is lowest, so the two genuinely travel together.
striga_vs_nitrogen.a_tell: Striga is a weed you can see. Small purple or pink flowering plants come up between the crop rows, and the crop nearest them is the most stunted, often wilting even when there is moisture in the soil. The damage is worst in patches around the striga plants.
striga_vs_nitrogen.b_tell: A nitrogen shortage has nothing growing between the rows. The crop pales evenly from the oldest leaves up, across the whole field or across the poorer part of it, with no purple flowering weed present.
striga_vs_nitrogen.decider: Get down and look between the rows before the crop closes over. If purple flowering weeds are attached around the crop roots, it is striga, and by the time you see them above ground the damage below is already done.
striga_vs_nitrogen.why_it_matters: Fertiliser alone will not clear striga, and pulling striga alone will not fix the fertility that let it establish. The two are handled together.
striga_vs_nitrogen.control: For striga: hand pull before it flowers and seeds, rotate and intercrop with legumes that make it germinate and die without a host, and raise fertility. For nitrogen: topdress and band beside the plant.

blossomendrot_vs_disease.both: Both spoil tomato fruit and both get sprayed, but only one of them is caused by something a spray can reach.
blossomendrot_vs_disease.a_tell: Blossom end rot is a disorder, not an infection. It makes a flat sunken leathery dark patch exactly at the blossom end of the fruit, the end away from the stalk, and it appears on fruit at the same growth stage across the plant. It comes from irregular watering and poor calcium uptake.
blossomendrot_vs_disease.b_tell: A fruit rot is an infection. The damage starts anywhere on the fruit, often at a wound or where fruit touches soil, it is soft or sunken with visible spore growth or rings, and it spreads from fruit to fruit.
blossomendrot_vs_disease.decider: Where on the fruit is it. Only at the blossom end, dry and leathery, on many fruit at once, is blossom end rot. Anywhere else, spreading, with mould or specks, is an infection.
blossomendrot_vs_disease.why_it_matters: Nothing sprayed will stop blossom end rot. It is fixed by watering evenly and mulching so the plant can take up calcium steadily.
blossomendrot_vs_disease.control: For blossom end rot: water regularly rather than in heavy irregular soakings, mulch to hold moisture even, and avoid heavy nitrogen which makes it worse. For fruit rots: stake fruit off the soil, remove and destroy affected fruit, and harvest promptly.

newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.both: Both kill birds quickly in a village flock and both are often called simply a fever, but one is a virus you prevent by vaccinating and the other is a parasite you prevent by keeping litter dry.
newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.a_tell: Newcastle is a virus and it hits the whole flock at once. Birds go quiet and off feed, there is greenish watery droppings, gasping and sneezing, and then twisted necks, paralysis or birds circling. Mortality sweeps through the house and vaccinated birds are the ones left standing.
newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.b_tell: Coccidiosis is a gut parasite and it shows in the droppings. Blood or dark reddish brown material in the droppings, birds hunched with ruffled feathers, pale combs, and it concentrates in chicks on damp litter and around the drinkers.
newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.decider: Look at the droppings and the nervous signs. Blood in the droppings with no nervous signs is coccidiosis. Greenish droppings with twisted necks or paralysis is Newcastle.
newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.why_it_matters: Newcastle has no treatment once it is in the flock and is prevented only by vaccination on schedule. Coccidiosis is treatable and is largely prevented by dry litter and clean water, so a wrong diagnosis wastes the one window you had.
newcastle_vs_coccidiosis.control: Vaccinate against Newcastle on the schedule your veterinary or extension officer gives, keep new birds separate before adding them to the flock, keep litter dry and drinkers clean, and take a bird showing nervous signs or bloody droppings to a veterinary officer, who will confirm it and advise the product and dose.

maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.both: Both leave pale yellow maize, and both are commonly answered with fertiliser.
maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.a_tell: Maize streak makes fine pale stripes that run the length of the leaf, parallel to the veins, broken and narrow rather than a wash of colour. It appears on individual plants scattered through the field, and those plants are badly stunted while their neighbours are fine.
maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.b_tell: A nitrogen shortage colours the whole leaf, and in maize it runs down the midrib from the tip as a V. It affects the field or a whole part of the field evenly, not scattered single plants.
maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.decider: Stripes along the leaf on scattered individual plants is the virus. An even wash of yellow, worst on the oldest leaves, across a whole area of the field, is nitrogen.
maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.why_it_matters: There is no cure for maize streak and fertiliser will not bring an infected plant back. The response is variety choice and planting time for next season.
maizestreak_vs_nitrogen.control: For maize streak: plant tolerant varieties, plant early and uniformly with the community so the crop is past its vulnerable stage when leafhopper numbers build, and remove volunteer maize and grass hosts around the field. For nitrogen: topdress and band beside the plant.
